evidence: Kew/POWO accepts Verbena canescens and lists Texas within its native range.
Hays County — the project Hays County native-source list includes Verbena canescens.
Travis County — the UT Plant Resources Center Travis County Verbenaceae index includes a Verbena canescens specimen.
Kerr County — the Kerr WMA vascular flora documents Verbena canescens repeatedly without an introduced marker.
target_zone_range.guardrail: Regional Edwards Plateau distribution alone is not used as a county substitute; the three listed counties have explicit local records.

morphology.look_here_first: Look for the gray cast before anything else: this is the short, low vervain whose stems and leaves are densely covered in stiff whitish hairs, giving the entire plant a canescent or dusty-gray appearance.
diagnostic_traits: low perennial, commonly under about 30 cm in the Williamson County treatment
stems and leaves densely hirsute/canescent, producing a gray-green appearance
opposite sessile to subsessile leaves, elliptic to oblong or nearly linear
leaf margins with only a few teeth or short lobes rather than deep major divisions
calyx and rachis conspicuously hairy, including pustulate-based hairs
four one-seeded mericarps with strongly pitted outer faces

confusers.separator: V. halei is greener and much less densely hairy, with lower leaves often deeply pinnatifid; V. canescens is uniformly gray/canescent and low.
V. xutha is taller/coarser, usually with obvious 3-lobed leaves and stronger pustulate/glandular hairiness.
V. scabra is far larger, with broad sandpaper-textured leaves and long panicles of spikes.
